analysis.one_liner: Lets patients bypass insurers' 'try a cheaper drug first' rules when the cheaper drug won't work for them.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Safe Step Act, with 48 Senate cosponsors, never received a vote; it sat in the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many health plans use 'step therapy': before covering the drug your doctor prescribed, the plan makes you try cheaper alternatives first. This bill would amend the nation's employee benefits law to require employer-based group health plans to grant an exception when the required drugs already failed, are likely to fail, would cause harm, would interfere with work or daily life, or when the patient is already stable on the prescribed drug. It would also require plans to publish a clear, easy-to-find exception process and answer standard requests within 72 hours (24 hours when delay could seriously jeopardize health or life).
analysis.who_benefits: Patients on employer-sponsored health plans whose doctors prescribed a drug the plan refuses to cover until cheaper alternatives are tried first — including people who already tried and failed those alternatives, people for whom the alternatives are medically risky, people whose medications keep them able to work, and people stable on a drug who changed jobs or plans. Prescribers also gain a defined, time-limited appeal process instead of ad hoc denials.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans to grant an exception to step therapy when required treatments were ineffective, are expected to be ineffective with delay risking severe or irreversible harm, are contraindicated or likely to cause adverse reactions, would prevent the patient from working or performing daily activities, or when the patient is already stable on the prescribed drug.
Requires plans to run a clear, transparent exception process — posted publicly online — and bars them from demanding documentation beyond what is strictly necessary to decide the request.
Sets deadlines: plans must answer a standard exception request within 72 hours, and within 24 hours when the step-therapy protocol may seriously jeopardize the patient's life or health.
Locks in the patient's original cost-sharing terms, so getting the prescribed drug via an exception doesn't come at a higher out-of-pocket rate than when they enrolled.

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plans and the insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that administer them, which would lose some of the cost savings from making patients try cheaper drugs first; those costs would flow partly into higher premiums and employer plan costs. The mandate covers only employer-based group plans, so people on Medicare, Medicaid, or individual-market insurance get no federal exception right from this bill.

drawbacks.text: Step therapy exists to control drug costs: insurers and employers argue that allowing more first-line exceptions pushes patients toward costlier drugs sooner, which would raise premiums and employer plan costs that are ultimately borne by workers and consumers.

The bill covers only group health plans governed by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act; the tens of millions of people on Medicare, Medicaid, or individual-market plans would get no new federal exception right from this bill.

Exception categories include open-ended provisions — such as 'other circumstances as determined by the Secretary' — which employers and plan sponsors warned could invite broader overrides of utilization management beyond the bill's medical justifications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients affected, the benefit is concrete and medical: not being forced to fail on drugs their doctor already knows won't work, and getting a timely answer when health or livelihood is at stake. The cost is diffuse — somewhat higher plan spending that filters into premiums. The strongest honest objection is the bill's narrow reach: it fixes step therapy only in the employer-plan lane while leaving the same practice in Medicare, Medicaid, and the individual market untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up or reported it, so it never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced the Safe Step Act on March 2, 2023 with an original bipartisan group of 18 cosponsors, including Democrats, Republicans, and Independents.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which is the last action recorded before the 118th Congress ended.

By the end of the Congress the bill had drawn 48 cosponsors — 33 of 48 Senate Democrats, 13 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 2 of 4 Independents — but no committee markup, hearing action, or floor vote appears in its record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer health plans, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers keep their step-therapy programs and the savings from them unchanged; no patient gained a federal right to a step-therapy exception. The bill's bipartisan cosponsor list shows broad Senate support, but the committee that held the bill allowed none of it to move.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who kept step therapy

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Step Act and recruited an initial bipartisan group of 18 cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 48 of 97 other senators
for.role: Cosponsors (33 of 48 Senate Democrats, 13 of 49 Senate Republicans, 2 of 4 Independents)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill majority-of-the-chamber support, but the bill never reached a vote for them to act on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2023 and took no further action on it — no markup or report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines from the start — the original 18 cosponsors included 10 Republicans along with Democrats and Independents, and by the end the bill had 33 Democratic, 13 Republican, and 2 Independent cosponsors; no senator is recorded in opposition.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer plan administrators
industries.note: Step therapy is a cost-control tool that steers patients to cheaper drugs first; this bill would strip away some of that control by mandating exceptions and 72-hour (or 24-hour) deadlines. Insurers would absorb added drug spending that flows into premiums.

PBMs design and run step-therapy protocols for plans; a required exceptions process with tight timelines and limits on extra documentation narrows their discretion over which drugs patients can access.

industries.industry: Brand-name and other non-preferred drug makers
industries.note: Their drugs are the ones step therapy typically holds back; easier exceptions mean more patients can get them without trying cheaper alternatives first, expanding access but also pushing plan spending toward higher-priced drugs.
